title: Indian Army Pilots Execute Daring Helicopter Rescue at 18,600 Feet Near Nun Kun
excerpt: Army Aviation crew evacuated a casualty from a steep Ladakh slope with no landing space, balancing the helicopter on one skid in fading daylight.
body:
• Indian Army Aviation pilots evacuated a casualty from 18,600 feet near the Nun Kun massif in Ladakh on Saturday, operating at the edge of helicopter flight capability.
  • The crew stripped the aircraft of non-essential equipment and flew with minimal fuel to maximize lift in the thin high-altitude air.
  • With no flat landing area available, the pilots executed a one-skid landing on a steep slope in strong mountain winds during the day's last usable light window.
  • The Fire and Fury Corps called the mission a testament to the skill, courage, and compassion of Indian Army Aviation.

Indian Army Aviation pilots carried out a high-altitude casualty evacuation at 18,600 feet near the Nun Kun massif in Ladakh on Saturday, the Fire and Fury Corps announced on social media. The operation required the crew to land a helicopter on a steep mountain slope with one skid while battling strong winds and rapidly fading daylight.

Operating at the Edge of Flight

At 18,600 feet — roughly the altitude of Everest Base Camp — atmospheric density drops sharply, cutting engine performance and rotor lift. To make the mission viable, the crew stripped the helicopter of all non-essential equipment to reduce weight to the absolute minimum. The aircraft carried only enough fuel to reach the extraction point and return, sacrificing safety margin for the lift capacity needed at extreme altitude.

"In a daring rescue mission at 18,600 ft near Nun Kun, Indian Army Aviation pilots evacuated a casualty from an extremely challenging slope with no landing space and strong winds," the Fire and Fury Corps posted on X.

A One-Skid Landing

Upon reaching the casualty's position on a sheer mountain slope, the crew found no conventional landing spot. Strong mountain winds added to the challenge. The pilots held the helicopter in a precarious low hover and executed a technique requiring extraordinary precision — balancing the aircraft with just one skid touching the slope while the other hung over the void.

The patient was secured and loaded rapidly before the crew lifted off and descended safely. The entire operation took place during the last available landing window of the day, leaving no room for a second attempt.

The Nun Kun Massif

Nun Kun is a twin-peaked massif in the Zanskar Range of Ladakh, with Nun Peak rising to 23,409 feet — the highest mountain in the former state of Jammu and Kashmir. The area's extreme elevation, unpredictable weather, and remote terrain make any aviation operation there exceptionally dangerous. Indian Army Aviation units regularly operate in these conditions along the northern borders.

A Pattern of High-Altitude Capability

The rescue adds to Indian Army Aviation's record of high-altitude operations in the Himalayas and Karakoram ranges. The corps operates Cheetah and Chetak helicopters — light utility aircraft chosen specifically for their ability to function at extreme altitudes — as well as newer Advanced Light Helicopters from Hindustan Aeronautics Limited.

For the Indian diaspora, missions like these underscore the operational capability and dedication of India's armed forces in some of the world's most demanding terrain — a source of enduring national pride.

"The mission, undertaken at the last available landing window of the day, stands as a testament to the skill, courage and compassion of Indian Army Aviation."

— Fire and Fury Corps, Indian Army
